source.file: A prediction market test of the macroeconomic impact of global temperature shocks (Letter draft).docx

title: How Detrimental will Climate Change be to Society? Let’s put the Question to a Prediction Market

runs.t: The economic impact of climate change has been estimated quantitatively since the 1970s
, and its severity has been disputed ever since
. Some general-audience and academic treatments describe scenarios of societal collapse
. Others have argued that economic and technological progress allows adaptation that offsets the negative impacts of warming and, in most cases, outpaces them

. The wide range of views is represented quantitatively in the wide range of published estimates of the social cost of carbon, the present value of the damage done by one additional ton of carbon dioxide, which still span several orders of magnitude

. Although the range is wide, it has a long tail on the severe end, and most studies have found that warming acts as a modest drag on growth. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change summarized the estimates available in 2014 as a loss of 0.2–2.0% of global annual income for about 2 °C of additional warming

These relatively benign economic impact calculations have perpetually frustrated activists in the climate movement who feel they should be higher. For example, when William Nordhaus won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Economics
for pioneering the field of climate-economics (and advocating a carbon tax to curb emissions along the way
), the decision was met with hostility from the climate movement
because Nordhaus’s representation of climate change's economic impact was considered insufficiently severe.
A distillation of the controversy has recently been embodied by a high-profile study by economists Adrien Bilal of Stanford and Diego Känzig of Northwestern (Bilal and Känzig 2026)
, which opens with:

“Climate change is frequently described as one of the defining economic challenges of our time. This view, however, stands in sharp contrast to empirical estimates of its impact on economic activity: they imply that a permanent 1ºC rise in temperature reduces world output by 1%–3%.”
They go on to say,
“In this article, we show that the macroeconomic effects of climate change are an order of magnitude larger than previously documented.”
And
“Our estimates imply that a permanent 1°C rise in global temperature lowers world GDP by over 20%.”
“Our results point to significant economic costs of climate change. They are comparable to the U.S. Great Depression of 1929, but experienced permanently.”
This research, first published as a preprint
, was widely celebrated

by those in the climate movement for finally giving academic weight to their intuition about the existential dangers of climate change. In fact, one of the coauthors themselves, Diego Känzig, explained the value of the paper as such

“When we read the newspapers and when we listen to the scientists, climate change is always portrayed as this existential threat that poses significant risks to our lives, livelihoods, and also the economy, but then when you look at these previous estimates, it doesn't look too severe so that was a tension and it's why when we arrived at these estimates they aligned better with my priors.”
Later working papers have challenged the estimates. Curtin and Burgess

report that the estimates are sensitive to controls for low-frequency variation, and they argue that temperature variation from El Niño or volcanic eruptions need not affect the economy the way greenhouse warming does. Kahn
argues that shocks should be measured with the information available in real time and that a response estimated from past shocks may change as people learn and adapt.

This resembles the launch/continuation of a perpetually inconclusive controversy typical of academic disputes where claims are so model-dependent and imbued with assumptions (both in the narrow sense of parameter values and model structure and in the broader sense of the ethical values encoded into the models) that they can persist in tension infinitely because they are practically unfalsifiable.
However, Bilal and Känzig (2026) is a bit different than other climate-economic claims due to the confluence of three attributes:

items.t: Bilal and Känzig (2026) is part of a broader literature that attempts to quantify a general relationship between temperature and economic activity from natural variation in the historical record

. This means that if we observe large enough short-term (natural) fluctuations in global average temperature, Bilal and Känzig (2026) predict specific consequences for the economy within time horizons short enough to practically detect and measure.

Bilal and Känzig (2026)’s claimed impact of global temperature variations on economic output is so large that it should be directly detectable in raw global GDP per capita, provided that the causal global temperature fluctuation was large enough.
We are currently in the midst of perhaps the
short-term warming fluctuation in global average temperature in the instrumental record (Fig. 1a). The years 2023, 2024 and 2025 were the three warmest in NOAA’s record

. Measured the paper’s way, the global temperature shock of 2024, +0.35 °C, was the largest since at least 1953 (Fig. 1a). NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center put the chance that the El Niño now underway exceeds the strength of every El Niño since 1950 at 83% for October–December 2026
, and a forecast of 1.49 °C above the 1901–2000 average for 2027 implies a second shock of about +0.29 °C.

runs.t: Thus, the next few years offer a very unique opportunity to adjudicate one of the most important questions in economics and politics: How much does temperature change impact the global economy?
That is why I am introducing a ForecastEx prediction market contract customized to test the claims of Bilal and Känzig (2026).
The contract translates the ongoing spike in global temperature into a prediction for the global GDP per capita over the next several years. Specifically, the event question is:
Will world GDP per capita grow by more than 1.1% a year, on average, from 2026 to 2031?
I expand on the origin of the specific numbers below, including why the cutoff depends on how warm 2027 turns out - and introducing a conditional contract along the way.

items.t: A “No” outcome aligns with Bilal and Känzig (2026) and the climate movement's broader concerns.
A “Yes” outcome aligns with conventional climate economics and more sanguine views of climate change's impact on society.

runs.t: The idea is to use a prediction market to make a consequential claim more testable while reducing the pull toward any preferred conclusion
and, thus, motivated cognition (Fig. 2).
This contract resembles the famous Simon–Ehrlich wager
in that it forces precise terms and conditions on a debate that is typically dominated by adjectives, and it challenges adversaries to put their money where their mouth is.

If someone takes a strong rhetorical public position in this debate but is unwilling to purchase a contract aligned with it, it may be fair to question their true conviction. At a minimum, the reasons for declining would bring to the surface caveats that the public position leaves out. The pull toward a preferred conclusion operates on every side of this dispute.

The design meets two requirements. Its terms use only information available at listing, before any of the growth they measure has occurred, and they favor neither view. I take the paper’s estimates at face value.

The contract measures world GDP per capita at purchasing power parity, in constant 2021 international dollars, from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (series NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, world aggregate)
. The statistic is average annual growth from 2026 to 2031,
where

is world GDP per capita, with both years taken from the release current at the resolution time so that revisions that move both years cancel. Growth is not rounded, and a contract resolves “Yes” only if

is strictly above its threshold. If that release has no value for 2026 or 2031, ForecastEx reads the series again on the first business day of each following month until a release has both. A discontinued series goes to ForecastEx’s event review (Rule 415). Growth starts in 2026, the last full year before listing, so none of the outcome is known when the contracts list. A 2027 start would give J of 0.60. The contract settles on the series that most closely follows the paper’s GDP data among those published in time to settle it. The paper’s estimate is fitted on the Penn World Table, which cannot settle a contract in 2032 because its releases lag several years. Of the World Bank’s series, the PPP series tracks the Penn World Table’s world GDP per capita most closely, with five-year average growth 0.20 points a year apart (root mean square over windows ending 1995–2019). The World Bank’s published growth rate (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD.ZG), at market exchange rates, sits 0.37 points apart. The paper’s country panel gives very similar results with World Bank data (its App. Fig. B.11).

An unconditional ladder of the same question lists at 13 thresholds from 0.1% to 2.1% a year, with 1.1% as the headline contract (proposed code WGDPC). The three conditional contracts (proposed code ZGTWGDPC) apply to the cool, central and warm ranges of NOAA’s 2027 value. ForecastEx’s Global Temperature (GT) contracts for 2027 at 1.45 and 1.53 °C decide the range, and ForecastEx lists their resolution for 14 January 2028

. Positions in the matching conditional contract then convert into the ladder at the same threshold and cost, and positions in the other two are refunded, which is how ForecastEx’s conditional contracts work. The terms would be fixed when NOAA publishes its 2026 annual value in mid-January 2027, and the contracts would list right after on ForecastEx, an exchange registered with the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission. All contracts resolve on 1 October 2032, about three months after the World Bank’s first estimate for 2031 (Fig. 3). Table 1 summarizes the terms, and the full terms are in the repository.
Temperatures are NOAA’s annual global land and ocean surface temperature (NOAAGlobalTemp, from Climate at a Glance) relative to the 1901–2000 average

. NOAA’s record is one of the two the paper uses, and the authors report that their Berkeley Earth measure correlates virtually perfectly with it and that the two give virtually identical results in their country panel

. NOAA publishes monthly and issues each annual value in January, and ForecastEx’s GT contracts resolve on it. Year-to-year changes since 1950 have averaged about 0.1 °C in either direction, and the El Niño–Southern Oscillation is their largest single source
The paper defines a global temperature shock as the departure of a year’s temperature from the value predicted by the temperatures two and three years earlier
. I fit that filter to NOAA’s record over the paper’s window (dependent years 1953–2022, with data from 1950) and hold its coefficients fixed,
where
is the annual temperature and

the shock, with a residual standard deviation of 0.12 °C. The shocks of 2023 onward are therefore measured out of sample. Over 1960–2019 they correlate at 0.99 with the authors’ published shocks (Fig. 1a). The 2024 shock of +0.35 °C exceeds the largest in the fitting window, +0.27 °C in 2016, and the 2023 shock of +0.22 °C is the third largest since 1953. Because the filter predicts 2026 from the record-warm years of 2023 and 2024, 2026 registers almost no shock (−0.01 °C), although it is likely to be the second-warmest year on record. Until NOAA publishes the annual values, 2026 is a nowcast from nine observed months (1.21 ± 0.02 °C) and 2027 a forecast from the expected strength of the El Niño (1.49 ± 0.10 °C, one standard deviation), which implies a 2027 shock of +0.29 °C. Refitting the filter through 2025 would shrink each tested shock by 0.04–0.05 °C and the predicted shortfall to 5.0 points (J = 0.62).

The paper estimates the response of world GDP per capita to a global temperature shock with time-series local projections on the Penn World Table (1960–2019). I re-estimated its response from the authors’ replication files, and the result matches the authors’ own output to within 10

percentage points (Fig. 5). The response reaches −12.1% six years after a 1 °C shock. I use the time-series estimate because it describes world GDP per capita, the quantity the contract measures. The paper’s headline panel estimate of 14% weights every country equally, and weighting countries by GDP gives −9.9% at year 6 (the paper’s App. Fig. B.10). Observed shocks are usually 0.1–0.2 °C, so the response to an observed shock is proportionally smaller.

The paper’s regression controls for the two preceding shocks, so its response applies to the part of each shock that those shocks do not predict. I apply it the same way. Applying it to raw shocks would count part of each shock twice and widen the predicted gap to 6.6 points, and reading it as the effect of transitory warmth only narrows the gap to 2.8 points. The response is held at its year-10 value beyond ten years. Each simulated path draws the response from the authors’ bootstrap distribution, so the simulations carry the paper’s statistical uncertainty. The sensitivity analysis uses seven other estimates from the same replication files (Supplementary Section 1).

The no-effect path is the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projection of world real GDP growth less world population growth, adjusted by the mean 1991–2025 difference between the World Bank’s and the IMF’s world growth (−0.07 percentage points)
. It has world GDP per capita growing by 2.4% in 2027, 2.3% in 2028 and 2029, 2.2% in 2030 and 2.1% in 2031, an average of 2.26% a year (Fig. 6). Along each path,
where
is the projected growth and
the path’s cumulative miss from 2026 to year

World growth is hard to predict years ahead. Over the five-year windows that followed each October forecast from 1990 to 2020, world growth came in 3.1 percentage points below the IMF’s forecast on average (about 0.6 points a year), and it fell short in 27 of the 31 windows

. The baseline keeps this average miss, so IMF optimism alone cannot push the contract toward the paper. Its spread comes from the same record, with each path taking one historical forecast’s whole sequence of misses, so that recessions and slowdowns keep their persistence (Supplementary Section 1). With no temperature effect, average growth from 2026 to 2031 is about 1.6% a year, with an 80% range of 1.0–2.3%. If the IMF’s forecasts have since become unbiased, the threshold is too low, and the central contract would resolve “No” only about half the time even if the paper is right.

The growth that would occur with no temperature effect is the largest judgment call in the design. The alternative trend baseline extends the average growth of world GDP per capita over a window that ends in 2019, before the pandemic, and draws its spread from the same years. For windows that open between 1991 and 2005, the average runs from 1.90% to 2.36% a year, the best threshold from 1.27% to 1.78% and J from 0.63 to 0.71 (Fig. 7). The 1.1% contract would then resolve “Yes” in 25–47% of the simulations in which the paper is right. The slow growth of the early 1990s pulls the average down for windows that open before 1994. Windows that open in 2010 or later hold no recession, and their spread would give J of 0.91–0.96, so the scan stops at 2005. I use the IMF’s projection because it is external to this analysis, fixed before listing and corrected for a bias documented over three decades.
Under the paper’s estimates, world GDP per capita follows the same background path less the response to every global temperature shock since 2015,
where
is the part of year
’s shock that the two shocks before it do not predict,
is the paper’s response after
years and

is the netting term described below. All shocks since 2015 count because, if the paper is right, the 2023–2025 shocks affect the same years as the El Niño, so the outcome carries them either way. The IMF’s past misses include whatever effect past temperature shocks had on growth. In the paper’s world the background therefore leaves out the part of those misses that the paper’s estimates attribute to temperature shocks, 0.9 of the 3.1 points, so that the damage is not counted twice. Without this netting the predicted gap would be 6.8 points, and the contract would overstate its chance of resolving the paper’s way. Over 2026–2031, before the netting, the shocks of 2026–2027 contribute −3.8 points (about 55% of the total), those of 2023–2025 contribute −2.6 points (37%) and those of 2015–2022 contribute −0.5 points (7%).

Taken at face value, the paper’s estimates imply that world GDP per capita will grow by about 0.5% a year from 2026 to 2031 (80% range, −0.5% to 1.4%), against about 1.6% a year with no temperature effect (Fig. 1). In constant 2021 international dollars, world GDP per capita would rise from about $21,900 in 2025 to about $23,100 in 2031 under the paper’s estimates and to about $24,500 with no temperature effect. The world keeps getting richer under both views.

Every later shock also moves GDP under the paper’s estimates, so the prediction includes simulated temperatures for 2028 onward. If a path’s 2027 winter is a strong El Niño (a December–February Relative Oceanic Niño Index of 1.5 °C or more), its later winters replay the winters that followed one of the seven strong El Niños since 1950 (1958, 1966, 1973, 1983, 1992, 1998 and 2016). Otherwise the index follows a second-order autoregression fitted to the winters since 1951. Each year’s shock is the prediction of a regression of shocks on the winter index in that year and the two before it, plus a residual resampled from 1953–2025, volcanic years included, so eruptions occur at their historical rate. The simulated shocks are then measured with the paper’s filter.

Strong El Niños are usually followed by cooler years (Fig. 8). Measured against the paper’s filter, which was fitted before the 2023–2024 jump, even a typical year after the El Niño sits slightly above expectation. The simulated years therefore change the predicted shortfall in 2031 by only 0.05 percentage points on average, and without them the best threshold would be 1.10% a year with J of 0.69. The temperatures in Fig. 1a follow from each path’s shocks through equation (2). Their medians for 2028–2031 are 1.28, 1.29, 1.48 and 1.39 °C. The 2030 value is high because equation (2) predicts each year from the temperatures two and three years earlier, with about half its weight on each, which carries the 2027 peak into 2030, and because the simulated 2030 shocks average +0.08 °C. The thresholds account for these years in advance and will not change once the temperatures of 2028–2031 are known.

I simulated 50,000 paths of world GDP per capita under each view, with common random numbers. The no-effect paths draw background growth from the IMF’s record of misses. The paper’s paths add the paper’s response, drawn from its bootstrap distribution, to the shocks of 2015–2027 and to the simulated shocks after 2027. For each candidate end year from 2028 to 2037, I found the threshold on average growth that maximizes Youden’s J
, which weighs an incorrect resolution under either view equally,

blocks.tex: J = P(No \mid paper\ right) + P(Yes \mid no\ effect) - 1.

runs.t: The threshold is the median of the candidate thresholds whose J is within 0.0025 of the best, which keeps Monte Carlo noise out of it. The end year is the one with the highest J to two decimals, with ties going to the earlier year. J is highest for 2031 (0.68), narrowly ahead of 2030 (0.67; Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 1). A longer period accumulates more of the paper’s predicted damage. However, uncertainty about background growth also grows with every added year, and after 2031 the effects of the 2023–2024 shocks begin to fade in the paper’s estimates. A period long enough to reach the trough of the paper’s response to the 2027 shock, which would end in 2033, separates the two views less well (J = 0.46). These choices use only information available before listing and no GDP data after 2025. At the 1.1% threshold, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve is 0.91.

At 1.1% a year, the contract resolves “No” in 82% of the simulations in which the paper is right and “Yes” in 87% of those in which temperature shocks have no effect (Fig. 10a). Whichever view is true, the contract resolves in line with it more than four times in five (J = 0.68).

The best threshold depends on how warm 2027 turns out, because a warmer 2027 means a larger predicted shortfall, and NOAA will not publish its 2027 value until January 2028. I therefore propose three conditional contracts. Their ranges divide the current forecast for 2027 into three about equally likely parts, with boundaries at 1.45 and 1.53 °C, halfway between its 20th, 50th and 80th percentiles (1.41, 1.49 and 1.58 °C). Within each range, the threshold maximizes J and is rounded to 0.1 point. That gives 1.2% a year if 2027 is cool (1.45 °C or lower), 1.1% if it falls in the central range (1.46–1.53 °C) and 1.0% if it is warm (1.54 °C or higher). J is 0.63, 0.69 and 0.74 for the three ranges, and each range has a chance of about one in three under today’s forecast (Fig. 10b). The cool range separates the views least, and a low-power clause for it remains open for comment until the terms are fixed. A contract written after NOAA publishes its 2027 value would take its threshold from Fig. 11, in which the best threshold falls from 1.21% a year at 1.30 °C to 0.99% at 1.70 °C.

The online version recomputes every figure under alternative settings of 14 controls. They cover the paper’s estimate (eight estimates, the share of its effect that is real and four treatments of its uncertainty), background growth (the IMF projection or the trend baseline with its start year, the share of the IMF’s average miss kept, the spread and the netting), temperatures (NOAA’s 2027 and 2026 values, the years after 2027 and the shocks counted) and the contract (end year and strike). The page re-runs the model in the reader’s browser on the same paths as the published run and changes only what a control names. At the published settings it reproduces the run to within 0.002 points of GDP on every path. Fig. 12 and Table 2 give the published design and 22 alternatives, each at the 1.1% strike and at its own best threshold, and on the online version each row sets the controls to it.

The separation holds under most of them. Across the paper’s eight estimates, the best threshold runs from 1.06% to 1.30% a year and J from 0.40 to 0.74. The estimates from the long Barro–Ursúa sample and from the transitory part of each shock separate the views least.

A contract on a stated event settles at $1 if the event occurs and at zero otherwise, so its price can be read as a probability, and prices aggregate dispersed information as they update until resolution
. Market prices have forecast elections and the replication of published experiments as well as or better than polls and surveys
, and a public market on daily temperatures has been more accurate than operational weather forecasts

In the central contract, the chance of “Yes” is about 18% if the paper is right and about 87% if temperature shocks have no effect. Where the price settles between those two values gives a running public measure of the credence informed participants give the paper’s estimate. Prices in prediction markets approximate the mean belief of participants under common conditions
, although the correspondence is not exact
. The two chances are each view’s share of the simulated paths.
After each question, the label gives the side likely to raise it and whether the design addresses it, it was checked or it remains a caveat.
Why does the contract use the paper’s 12% estimate when its headline is 14%?
(paper’s side; addressed)

The contract is on world GDP per capita, and the paper’s estimate for world GDP is its time-series result (its Fig. III, about 12% six years after a 1 °C shock). The 14% is the country-panel average, which weights every country equally. Weighting countries by their share of world GDP, as the paper does in its App. Fig. B.10, gives −9.9% at year 6. Using the 14% moves the gap between the two views from 5.9 to 6.3 points and the threshold from 1.09% to 1.08% a year (J 0.68 and 0.70). With the GDP-weighted panel they are 4.5 points and 1.20% (J 0.58).
Was the shock filter fitted on the very years being tested?
(paper’s side; addressed)

No. The filter is fitted on the paper’s own window (dependent years 1953–2022, data from 1950), so the 2023–2027 warmth is measured out of sample. Refitting through 2025 shrinks each tested shock by about 0.04–0.05 °C and the gap to 5.0 points (J 0.62).
Does the no-effect background already contain the paper’s damage?
(paper’s side; addressed)

In part, and the design takes that part out. By the paper’s own estimates, 0.9 of the IMF’s average 3.1-point miss over five-year windows came from temperature shocks, since warming ran ahead of its trend after 1990. In the paper’s world that part is taken out of the background, because the paper’s damage enters through the shocks since 2015. Without this, the gap would be 6.8 points and the contract would overstate its chance of resolving the paper’s way.
Why does the contract use NOAA temperatures and World Bank GDP when the estimate it tests uses Berkeley Earth and the Penn World Table?
(paper’s side; addressed)

NOAA’s record is the paper’s own temperature series for its sample from 1860, and ForecastEx’s GT contracts, on which the conditional contracts depend, resolve on NOAA’s value. The paper reports that its Berkeley Earth measure correlates virtually perfectly with NOAA’s, and that NOAA’s record gives virtually identical results in its country panel (its App. Fig. B.11). The Penn World Table cannot settle a contract in 2032, because its latest release, of October 2025, ends in 2023. The paper uses World Bank data as its alternative, and its country panel gives very similar results with them. The contract settles on the World Bank’s PPP series, which tracks the Penn World Table most closely (see Contract and resolution). The paper does not report its world time series with either substitute. Re-estimating that series with the authors’ NOAA data gives −11.6% six years after a shock, against −12.1% with the paper’s data, and with the authors’ world GDP from World Bank data, at market exchange rates, −12.7%. The thresholds become 1.10% and 1.06% a year, against 1.09%.
Does the growth period end before the El Niño’s full effect?
(paper’s side; caveat)

Yes. The paper’s response peaks six years after a shock, after 2031 for the 2027 shock. The end year is set by a fixed rule that maximizes the separation between the two views, and longer periods add more background uncertainty than predicted damage (Supplementary Table 1).
Does linear scaling break down for shocks this large?
(paper’s side; caveat)

The paper finds no sign that it does. The 2024 shock (0.35 °C) is 31% larger than the largest in the filter’s 1953–2022 sample (0.27 °C, 2016), and the 2027 shock may be as well. The paper finds no sign that larger shocks have smaller effects, and positive shocks have effects at least as large as negative ones (its App. Fig. B.6). Linear scaling is therefore unlikely to overstate the paper’s predicted damage.
Does El Niño warmth differ from the global temperature variation the paper studied?
(paper’s side; addressed)

The paper reports almost the same estimate after controlling for the same year’s Oceanic Niño Index or for volcanic eruptions (its App. Fig. B.9) and says its results hold across sources of temperature variation. El Niño heat shows up first in the oceans, and the paper finds that ocean temperature drives most of the effect (its Fig. IX). Curtin and Burgess

argue that temperature variation from El Niño need not affect the economy the way greenhouse warming does. That argument bears on the use of the paper’s estimates for permanent warming. The contract tests the paper’s estimated response to global temperature shocks, which is what the paper measures. The years after the El Niño are simulated with the cooling that usually follows a strong one, and measured with the paper’s filter they change the predicted gap by −0.05 points.
Has adaptation since 2019 weakened the effect?
(paper’s side; caveat)
It may have. The paper reports no sign of adaptation, with estimates stable across periods, and presents them as the effect absent new adaptation. Curtin and Burgess
dispute this with smaller Penn World Table estimates in later rolling windows, and Kahn
argues that the effect fades as people adapt. A “Yes” could mean that the estimate is too high or that adaptation has improved, and the contract cannot tell which.
If the IMF has become less optimistic, are the strikes too low?
(paper’s side; caveat)

Yes. The no-effect expectation keeps the IMF’s average past miss. If the IMF’s forecasts are now unbiased, the central contract would resolve “No” only 51% of the time when the paper is right, against 82%.
Would one-step-ahead temperature shocks change the answer?
(paper’s side; checked)

Only a little. The paper reports similar responses with one-step shocks (its Fig. V and App. Fig. B.13). With one-step shocks and the matching response, the shocks’ effect on 2026–2031 growth is 5.9 points, against 6.8 with the paper’s two-step shocks (central temperatures, no shocks after 2027, before the netting).
Could a recession with an obvious cause outside the climate make the paper look right?
(other side; caveat)

Yes, and the paper would then look right for the wrong reason. A downturn with an obvious cause outside the climate, such as the 2008–2009 financial crisis or the 2020 pandemic, cuts world growth whatever global temperature does. In the World Bank series the contract settles on, world GDP per capita fell by 1.9% in 2009 and by 3.8% in 2020. Its average growth from 2015 to 2020 was 1.0% a year, below the 1.1% threshold. A recession like these late in the growth period, with little time to recover before 2031, could make the contract resolve “No” and the paper look right by the numbers even though temperature played little part. Such a “No” would say little about the paper’s estimate, because the cause of the shortfall would be plain. The paper’s own main identification concern is the same kind of coincidence, a severe El Niño arriving with an unrelated global recession. The spread of background growth includes such episodes, since the IMF’s record covers 2009 and 2020, which is why the contract resolves “No” 13% of the time even with no temperature effect. A recession clause is not possible, because under the paper’s estimates temperature shocks themselves cut investment and productivity.
Is the no-effect baseline a judgment call?
(other side; caveat)

It is the largest one. A trend baseline from a window that ends in 2019 puts the threshold at 1.27–1.78% a year, against 1.09% (Fig. 7). The IMF projection is external and fixed at October 2026, and its spread is the IMF’s own forecast record.
Does it matter that part of the 2023–2024 warmth had unusual causes, such as cleaner shipping fuel, the Hunga Tonga eruption and the solar maximum?
(other side; caveat)
The contract uses NOAA’s measured temperature, whatever its cause, and the paper finds similar effects across sources of temperature variation (its App. Fig. B.9).
Would applying the response to raw shocks, or to one-year warmth only, give a different prediction?
(other side; checked)

Yes, and the design applies it as the paper estimates it. The paper’s regression controls for the two previous shocks, so its response applies to the part of each shock they do not predict. Raw shocks would count part of each shock twice and give a gap of 6.6 points. Reading the response as one-year warmth only (its App. Fig. B.5) gives 2.8.
Is the paper’s estimate less precise than its bands suggest?
(both sides; checked)

If it is, the threshold barely moves. The paper-side spread comes from bootstrap draws of the paper’s response. Rescaled to the paper’s Newey–West standard errors, they give a threshold of 1.10% a year (J 0.66). Widened by half, they give 1.09% (J 0.64), against 1.09% (J 0.68). With the wider draws, the chance of a “No” if the paper is right falls from 81% to 77%.
Can one episode confirm or refute the paper?
(both sides; caveat)

No. The contract resolves against the true view about one time in six, and the separation is moderate (J 0.68), so a result adds to the weight of evidence and leaves the question open. Prices show how much credence participants give the paper.
What if the World Bank rebases its price comparisons (PPPs) before resolution?
(both sides; caveat)
Both years come from the same data release, so level revisions cancel. Country weights can still shift growth slightly, and the paper’s results are similar across GDP sources.
Does the IMF’s October 2026 projection already include some El Niño effects?
(both sides; caveat)

If it does, the no-effect expectation is slightly too low, which tilts the contract toward “Yes”. IMF projections rarely quantify global temperature effects, and this has not yet been checked against the projection’s text.

These caveats notwithstanding, the contract turns a long-running dispute into a dated, public test whose terms are fixed before any of the data exist. Its price would show from January 2027 how much credence informed participants give the estimate, and its resolution in October 2032 would add a known amount of evidence on how much global temperature affects the world economy.

Temperature data are from NOAA’s Climate at a Glance (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/global/time-series), and the Oceanic Niño Index is from NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center. GDP data are from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD). The IMF projection and forecast record are from the IMF DataMapper and the Historical WEO Forecasts Database. The authors’ replication files are at https://github.com/dkaenzig/micc_replication. The repository records every retrieval date and file hash.

The code and the full contract terms are at https://github.com/ptbrown31/climate-gdp-contract under the MIT license. The online version at https://weather.weatherclimatehumansystems.org/climate-gdp.html re-runs the analysis under alternative assumptions and links each figure’s method note to the code that computes it.

P.T.B. conceived the contracts, wrote the code and wrote the manuscript.

I am employed by Trend Analytics, LLC, a subsidiary of Interactive Brokers Group, which owns and operates ForecastEx, the exchange on which the proposed contracts would list. I have argued, with co-authors who include two of the critics cited here

, that adaptation will offset much of the negative impact of warming, so a “Yes” outcome would be welcome to me. As in much research, some questions and framings are more appealing to their authors than others, and that is the case here. I chose the end year and the threshold by a criterion that weighs both views equally, and every input and line of code is public so that others can check them.
Supplementary Information is available for this paper. Correspondence and requests for materials should be addressed to P.T.B. (pabrown@interactivebrokers.com).
Temperatures for 2026 and 2027.

Until NOAA publishes a year’s annual value, the analysis carries an estimate with its uncertainty. The 2026 nowcast combines the months NOAA has published with the rest of the year, estimated from the change between those months and the rest in seven past El Niño onset years. The 2027 forecast adds the shock predicted from the winter Relative Oceanic Niño Index in 2027 and the two winters before it to what the paper’s filter expects for 2027. Within a range of NOAA’s 2027 value, a path’s 2027 temperature is drawn from the forecast cut to that range.
The IMF’s record of misses.
The IMF’s October forecasts of 1990–2020 (31 forecasts) missed world growth by 3.1 points on average over the statistic’s years. Each path’s miss in year

The paper’s estimates.

Each estimate has 4,000 draws. For the time series they are the authors’ wild bootstrap, re-centred on the estimate. For the country panels they are normal draws with the paper’s band-implied standard errors and the time series’ correlation across horizons, an approximation. The Newey–West option rescales the time-series draws to the paper’s Newey–West standard errors, and the widened option scales their spread by 1.5. The estimates from the Barro–Ursúa sample use the paper’s filter with six lags of temperature, as the paper does, fitted on NOAA data from 1850.
Thresholds and densities.

Each best threshold is the median of the candidate thresholds whose J is within 0.0025 of the best. The densities in Fig. 10a are Gaussian kernel estimates with a bandwidth of 0.18 times the sample’s standard deviation.
The online version.

The page reads each path’s IMF misses, bootstrap draw, 2026–2027 temperatures and simulated shocks after 2027 from the published run and recomputes only what a control changes. At the published settings it reproduces the run to within 0.002 points of GDP on every path, and the repository’s test checks twelve designs path by path.

subtitle: The Super El Niño of 2026-2027 offers a rare opportunity to shed some empirical light on one of the most persistent and consequential controversies in contemporary science and politics: How much harm does climate change do to the global economy?
